extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in logic, set theory, and philosophy of mathematics; educated general readers
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedia-style exposition of Russell's Paradox: its statement in terms of classes/properties, historical context, and the major proposed solutions in logic and set theory (type theory, stratification/NF, ZF separation, conservatism about properties, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Russell's Paradox (classes form)
rubrics_metrics.description: A contradiction arising from considering the class of all classes that are not members of themselves: asking whether this class is a member of itself yields 'it is if and only if it is not.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the paradox concretely as a self-referential contradiction in naive class/set formation; motivates why a universal class or unrestricted comprehension is problematic. Example/construction: the class of all classes not included in themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Russell's Paradox (properties form)
rubrics_metrics.description: A contradiction involving properties: consider the property that something has iff it is a property that does not apply to itself; asking whether this property applies to itself yields a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes the parallel between the class-version and the properties-version; frames properties as potential objects of self-application and highlights why naive commitment to a property for every predicate leads to trouble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor's power-class/diagonal argument as source of the paradox
rubrics_metrics.description: Russell's paradox can be seen as a simplification of the Cantorian diagonal/mapping argument: attempting to map entities to their subclasses leads to the subclass of those entities not in their mapped subclasses, producing a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the mapping/diagonal construction (1-1 mapping f from domain to subclasses, form the subclass of entities not in their image under f) as the structural mechanism producing the antinomy; use this to show why a universal class or naive comprehension clashes with Cantor's theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehension principle (naive abstraction) and its rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: The comprehension (class abstraction) principle: for every open formula there exists a class (or property) of all and only those things satisfying that formula. Naive unrestricted comprehension is identified as the source of the contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides one to avoid assuming unrestricted comprehension; motivates restrictive alternatives. The article notes Frege's and Russell's original commitment to comprehension and how that commitment must be weakened or abandoned to avoid paradox.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frege's weakening of the class abstraction principle (revised clause)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frege's proposed fix: conclude only that an object is in a class iff the object falls under the concept defining the class and the object is not identical to the class in question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes Frege's appendix response to Russell: add the non-identity requirement to block the class-version of the paradox; notes that Frege later found further complications and abandoned the approach because other contradictions remained possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of Types (for properties and classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Insist that properties and classes are stratified into different logical types so that a property (or class) can never take itself as an argument or be of the type that allows membership of itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains both Frege's levels-of-concept move and Russell's more comprehensive type-theory (dividing properties and classes into types). Notes philosophical work required to justify the type-division (e.g., Russell's appeal to the 'unsaturatedness' of concepts) and mentions ramified type-theory (Principia Mathematica) as a development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservatism about Properties (restricting metaphysical commitment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deny that a property exists for every specifiable condition or predicate; allow only a restricted class of 'simple' properties to be taken as objectively existing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presents this as a metaphysical/nominalist response: by refusing to reify arbitrary complex predicates as properties (e.g., 'having-seventeen-heads'), one avoids the problematic property 'being-a-property-that-does-not-apply-to-itself.' Notes nominalism as an extreme version and more moderate restrictions on comprehension as alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stratification (Quine's New Foundations, NF)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quine's approach: allow meaningful assertions like 'x is not a member of x' but restrict set existence to those definitional formulas that are stratified — variables can be assigned natural numbers so each membership lowers the number — thereby blocking the unstratified Russell-defining formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the stratification condition for formulas and states that NF thereby blocks Russell's construction. Also notes that whether NF is consistent remains an open question (at least historically), so this solution's technical status is delicate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aussonderung / Zermelo-Fraenkel (ZF) Separation (bottom-up approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: ZF avoids a universal set by building sets 'bottom-up' from individuals and the empty set and only allowing formation of subsets of already existing sets via a Separation (Aussonderung) principle, rather than unrestricted comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes the ZF method: no universal set is postulated, and for any existing set A and condition C one may form the subset of A satisfying C. This blocks the construction of 'the set of all sets not members of themselves' because no universal set exists to separate from. Mentions later developments by Bernays, Gödel, von Neumann.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ramified type-theory and later technical modifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Later expansions or modifications of the above solutions (e.g., ramified type theory in Principia Mathematica, Quine's later systems, and developments in set theory by Bernays, Gödel, and von Neumann) aim to address technical and philosophical problems raised by simpler fixes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treats these as technical refinements or alternative formal frameworks that attempt to preserve as much of naive set-theoretic practice as possible while blocking paradoxes. The article notes debate continues about which solution is 'correct.'
